Prophecy of the Destruction of the Corrupt "Princes of the People;" Pelatiah Dies; Promise of Grace to the Believing Remnant; Departure of the Glory of God from the City; Ezekiel's Return to the Captives.</title> <div sID="gen20038" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11116"/><hi type="bold">1. east gate--</hi>to which the glory of God had moved itself (<reference osisRef="Ezek.10.19">Eze 10:19</reference>), the chief entrance of the sanctuary; the portico or porch of Solomon. The Spirit moves the prophet thither, to witness, in the presence of the divine glory, a new scene of destruction.<div eID="gen20038" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20039" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">five and twenty men--</hi>The same as the twenty-five (that is, twenty-four heads of courses, and the high priest) sun-worshippers seen in <reference osisRef="Ezek.8.16">Eze 8:16</reference>. The leading priests were usually called "princes of the sanctuary" (<reference osisRef="Isa.43.28">Is 43:28</reference>) and "chiefs of the priests" (<reference osisRef="2Chr.36.14">2Ch 36:14</reference>); but here two of them are called "princes of the people," with irony, as using their priestly influence to be ringleaders of the people in sin (<reference osisRef="Ezek.11.2">Eze 11:2</reference>). Already the wrath of God had visited the people represented by the elders (<reference osisRef="Ezek.9.6">Eze 9:6</reference>); also the glory of the Lord had left its place in the holy of holies, and, like the cherubim and flaming sword in Eden, had occupied the gate into the deserted sanctuary. The judgment on the representatives of the priesthood naturally follows here, just as the sin of the priests had followed in the description (<reference osisRef="Ezek.8.12">Eze 8:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.8.16">16</reference>) after the sin of the elders.<div eID="gen20039" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20040" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Jaazaniah--</hi>signifying "God hears."<div eID="gen20040" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20041" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">son of Azur--</hi>different from Jaazaniah the son of Shaphan (<reference osisRef="Ezek.8.11">Eze 8:11</reference>). Azur means "help." He and Pelatiah ("God delivers"), son of Benaiah ("God builds"), are singled out as Jaazaniah, son of Shaphan, in the case of the seventy elders (<reference osisRef="Ezek.8.11">Eze 8:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.8.12">12</reference>), because their names ought to have reminded them that "God" would have "heard" had they sought His "help" to "deliver" and "build" them up. But, neglecting this, they incurred the heavier judgment by the very relation in which they stood to God [Fairbairn]. <div eID="gen20041" type="x-p"/>

But, neglecting this, they incurred the heavier judgment by the very relation in which they stood to God [Fairbairn].

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11118"/><div sID="gen20044" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11118"/><hi type="bold">3. It is not near--</hi>namely, the destruction of the city; therefore "let us build houses," as if there was no fear. But the Hebrew opposes English Version, which would require the infinitive absolute. Rather, "Not at hand is the building of houses." They sneer at Jeremiah's letter to the captives, among whom Ezekiel lived (<reference osisRef="Jer.29.5">Jr 29:5</reference>). "Build ye houses, and dwell in them," that is, do not fancy, as many persuade you, that your sojourn in Babylon is to be short; it will be for seventy years (<reference osisRef="Jer.25.11">Jr 25:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.25.12">12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.29.10">29:10</reference>); therefore build houses and settle quietly there. The scorners in Jerusalem reply, Those far off in exile may build if they please, but it is too remote a concern for us to trouble ourselves about [Fairbairn], (Compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.12.22">Eze 12:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.12.27">27</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.4">2Pe 3:4</reference>).<div eID="gen20044" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20045" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">this city ... caldron ... we ... flesh--</hi>sneering at <reference osisRef="Jer.1.13">Jr 1:13</reference>, when he compared the city to a caldron with its mouth towards the north. "Let Jerusalem be so if you will, and we the flesh, exposed to the raging foe from the north, still its fortifications will secure us from the flame of war outside; the city must stand for our sakes, just as the pot exists for the safety of the flesh in it." In opposition to this God says (<reference osisRef="Ezek.11.11">Eze 11:11</reference>), "This city shall not be your caldron, to defend you in it from the foe outside: nay, ye shall be driven out of your imaginary sanctuary and slain in the border of the land." "But," says God, in <reference osisRef="Ezek.11.7">Eze 11:7</reference>, "your slain are the flesh, and this city the caldron; but (not as you fancy, shall ye be kept safe inside) I will bring you forth out of the midst of it"; and again, in <reference osisRef="Ezek.24.3">Eze 24:3</reference>, "Though not a caldron in your sense, Jerusalem shall be so in the sense of its being exposed to a consuming foe, and you yourselves in it and with it." <div eID="gen20045" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11121"/><div sID="gen20049" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11121"/><hi type="bold">6. your slain--</hi>those on whom you have brought ruin by your wicked counsels. Bloody crimes within the city brought on it a bloody foe from without (<reference osisRef="Ezek.7.23">Eze 7:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.7.24">24</reference>). entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11129"/><div sID="gen20060" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11129"/><hi type="bold">15. thy brethren ... brethren--</hi>The repetition implies, "Thy real brethren" are no longer the priests at Jerusalem with whom thou art connected by the natural ties of blood and common temple service, but thy fellow exiles on the Chebar, and the house of Israel whosoever of them belong to the remnant to be spared.<div eID="gen20060" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20061" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">men of thy kindred--</hi>literally, "of thy redemption," that is, the nearest relatives, whose duty it was to do the part of Goel, or vindicator and redeemer of a forfeited inheritance (<reference osisRef="Lev.25.25">Le 25:25</reference>). Ezekiel, seeing the priesthood doomed to destruction, as a priest, felt anxious to vindicate their cause, as if they were his nearest kinsmen and he their Goel. But he is told to look for his true kinsmen in those, his fellow exiles, whom his natural kinsmen at Jerusalem despised, and he is to be their vindicator. Spiritual ties, as in the case of Levi (<reference osisRef="Deut.33.9">De 33:9</reference>), the type of Messiah (<reference osisRef="Matt.12.47-Matt.12.50">Mt 12:47-50</reference>) are to supersede natural ones where the two clash. The hope of better days was to rise from the despised exiles. The gospel principle is shadowed forth here, that the despised of men are often the chosen of God and the highly esteemed among men are often an abomination before Him (<reference osisRef="Luke.16.15">Lu 16:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.26-1Cor.1.28">1Co 1:26-28</reference>). "No door of hope but in the valley of Achor" ("trouble," <reference osisRef="Hos.2.15">Ho 2:15</reference>), [Fairbairn].<div eID="gen20061" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20062" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Get you far ... unto us is this land--</hi>the contemptuous words of those left still in the city at the carrying away of Jeconiah to the exiles, "However far ye be outcasts from the Lord and His temple, we are secure in our possession of the land." <div eID="gen20062" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 15. thy brethren ... brethren-- The repetition implies, "Thy real brethren" are no longer the priests at Jerusalem with whom thou art connected by the natural ties of blood and common temple service, but thy fellow exiles on the Chebar, and the house of Israel whosoever of them belong to the remnant to be spared. men of thy kindred-- literally, "of thy redemption," that is, the nearest relatives, whose duty it was to do the part of Goel, or vindicator and redeemer of a forfeited inheritance ( Le 25:25 ). Ezekiel, seeing the priesthood doomed to destruction, as a priest, felt anxious to vindicate their cause, as if they were his nearest kinsmen and he their Goel. But he is told to look for his true kinsmen in those, his fellow exiles, whom his natural kinsmen at Jerusalem despised, and he is to be their vindicator. Spiritual ties, as in the case of Levi ( De 33:9 ), the type of Messiah ( Mt 12:47-50 ) are to supersede natural ones where the two clash. The hope of better days was to rise from the despised exiles. The gospel principle is shadowed forth here, that the despised of men are often the chosen of God and the highly esteemed among men are often an abomination before Him ( Lu 16:15 ; 1Co 1:26-28 ). "No door of hope but in the valley of Achor" ("trouble," Ho 2:15 ), [Fairbairn]. Get you far ... unto us is this land-- the contemptuous words of those left still in the city at the carrying away of Jeconiah to the exiles, "However far ye be outcasts from the Lord and His temple, we are secure in our possession of the land."
entries.reader_content_plain: 15. thy brethren ... brethren-- The repetition implies, "Thy real brethren" are no longer the priests at Jerusalem with whom thou art connected by the natural ties of blood and common temple service, but thy fellow exiles on the Chebar, and the house of Israel whosoever of them belong to the remnant to be spared. men of thy kindred-- literally, "of thy redemption," that is, the nearest relatives, whose duty it was to do the part of Goel, or vindicator and redeemer of a forfeited inheritance ( Le 25:25 ). Ezekiel, seeing the priesthood doomed to destruction, as a priest, felt anxious to vindicate their cause, as if they were his nearest kinsmen and he their Goel. But he is told to look for his true kinsmen in those, his fellow exiles, whom his natural kinsmen at Jerusalem despised, and he is to be their vindicator. Spiritual ties, as in the case of Levi ( De 33:9 ), the type of Messiah ( Mt 12:47-50 ) are to supersede natural ones where the two clash. The hope of better days was to rise from the despised exiles. The gospel principle is shadowed forth here, that the despised of men are often the chosen of God and the highly esteemed among men are often an abomination before Him ( Lu 16:15 ; 1Co 1:26-28 ). "No door of hope but in the valley of Achor" ("trouble," Ho 2:15 ), [Fairbairn]. Get you far ... unto us is this land-- the contemptuous words of those left still in the city at the carrying away of Jeconiah to the exiles, "However far ye be outcasts from the Lord and His temple, we are secure in our possession of the land."

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11130"/><div sID="gen20063" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11130"/><hi type="bold">16. Although--</hi>anticipating the objection of the priests at Jerusalem, that the exiles were "cast far off." Though this be so, and they are far from the outer temple at Jerusalem, I will be their asylum or sanctuary instead (<reference osisRef="Ps.90.1">Psa 90:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.91.9">91:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.8.14">Is 8:14</reference>). My shrine is the humble heart: a preparation for gospel catholicity when the local and material temple should give place to the spiritual (<reference osisRef="Isa.57.15">Is 57:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.66.1">66:1</reference>; Mal 1:11; <reference osisRef="John.4.21-John.4.24">Joh 4:21-24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.7.48">Ac 7:48</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.7.49">49</reference>). The trying discipline of the exile was to chasten the outcasts so as to be meet recipients of God's grace, for which the carnal confidence of the priests disqualified them. The dispersion served the end of spiritualizing and enlarging the views even of the better Jews, so as to be able to worship God everywhere without a material temple; and, at the same time, it diffused some knowledge of God among the greatest Gentile nations, thus providing materials for the gathering in of the Christian Church among the Gentiles; so marvellously did God overrule a present evil for an ultimate good. Still more does all this hold good in the present much longer dispersion which is preparing for a more perfect and universal restoration (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.2-Isa.2.4">Is 2:2-4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.3.16-Jer.3.18">Jr 3:16-18</reference>). Their long privation of the temple will prepare them for appreciating the more, but without Jewish narrowness, the temple that is to be (Eze 40:1-44:31).<div eID="gen20063" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20064" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a little--</hi>rather, "for a little season"; No matter how long the captivity may be, the seventy years will be but as a little season, compared with their long subsequent settlement in their land. This holds true only partially in the case of the first restoration; but as in a few centuries they were dispersed again, the full and permanent restoration is yet future (<reference osisRef="Jer.24.6">Jr 24:6</reference>). <div eID="gen20064" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11136"/><div sID="gen20076" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11136"/>23. The Shekinah glory now moves from the east gate (<reference osisRef="Ezek.10.4">Eze 10:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.10.19">19</reference>) to the Mount of Olives, altogether abandoning the temple. The mount was chosen as being the height whence the missiles of the foe were about to descend on the city. So it was from it that Jesus ascended to heaven when about to send His judgments on the Jews; and from it He predicted its overthrow before His crucifixion (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.3">Mt 24:3</reference>). It is also to be the scene of His return in person to deliver His people (<reference osisRef="Zech.14.4">Zec 14:4</reference>), when He shall come by the same way as He went, "the way of the east" (<reference osisRef="Ezek.43.2">Eze 43:2</reference>). <div eID="gen20076" type="x-p"/>
